title: Sergius of Radonezh
hookLine: a Russian hermit in the forest who shared bread with a bear and founded a great monastery

lines: ONE PIECE OF BREAD ON A STUMP.
A CELL DEEP IN THE FOREST.
A BEAR COMES OUT OF THE TREES.
cards: One piece of bread, on a tree stump at the edge of a clearing. Deep in a Russian forest, a young man has built a small wooden cell and a chapel with his own hands. No village nearby, no road worth the name.
One day, the old account says, a bear comes out of the trees, hungry, and stands looking at him. He doesn't run. He brings out a piece of his bread and sets it on the stump.
The bear eats it and goes away. Then it comes back, again and again. Today: Sergius of Radonezh.

teach.h: A LIFE WRITTEN BY HIS DISCIPLE.
teach.b: Sergius is a monk the Russian Orthodox Church honors as a saint, and his story comes down through a Life written by a monk named Epiphanius.
As a young man, the Life says, Sergius went into the forest to live alone with God. He chopped his own wood, grew what he could, and prayed. And the bear kept coming.
Here's the detail the Life lingers on.
Some days Sergius had only one piece of bread, and on those days, the story goes, he gave it to the bear and went hungry himself, rather than send the animal away with nothing.
An odd kind of holiness: not a sermon, but a crust, and an empty stomach.
Other Christian stories, too, put holy people at peace with wild animals, and Mark's Gospel has a small line about Jesus in the desert, in the King James Bible: "and was with the wild beasts".
In these stories the wilderness isn't only danger; it's also where creatures and a person at prayer learn to live side by side. Sergius didn't stay alone.
Other monks heard of him and came to live near him, cells went up around his, and a community grew, dedicated to the Holy Trinity.

The Life remembers him as a leader who still carried water, baked bread and wore patched clothes. A monastery grew where his cell had been. But the scene that stays is smaller: the stump, the bread, and the bear.

how: The Russian Orthodox Church honors Sergius of Radonezh as a saint, and the Trinity monastery that grew up around his forest cell bears his name; his story with the bear is told in his Life.

games.q: you're a hermit in the forest. a bear comes to your clearing, hungry. today you have one piece of bread left. what do you do?
o: eat it yourself; the bear can find its own food.
give the bear your last piece and go hungry.
bar the door and wait for it to leave.
games.why: the Life says that on days like that, Sergius gave the bear his bread and went without.

practice: Think of an animal near your life, a pet on the couch, the birds outside, a neighbor's dog, and one small thing it could use: fresh water, a few seeds, a walk, or simply your patience.
Sit with that creature in mind, the way Sergius sat at the edge of his clearing. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, let it be in your thoughts, just as it is.
